title: Static Greeting
prompt: Build a functional component that renders a heading with a short greeting message.

steps: Place a greeting inside the heading.
approach.example: The component renders a heading containing 'Hello, React!' when displayed.

walkthroughSteps: Greeting defines a functional React component.
The return statement provides the JSX to render.
The h1 element displays the greeting text.
The default export makes Greeting available to other files.
commonMistakes: Returning plain text without wrapping it in JSX.
Forgetting to export the component as default.

title: Button Component
prompt: Build a functional component that renders a button with a visible label.

steps: Place a short label inside the button.
approach.example: The component displays a button labeled 'Click Me' on the page.

walkthroughSteps: ActionButton defines the component.
The returned JSX contains one button element.
The text between the button tags becomes its visible label.
The default export allows the component to be imported elsewhere.
commonMistakes: Using a self-closing button without its label.
Writing the component without a return statement.

title: Text Paragraph
prompt: Build a functional component that displays a short paragraph below a heading.

approach.example: The component displays 'About' as a heading followed by 'Learn React step by step.'

walkthroughSteps: About defines the functional component.
section provides one parent element for the returned JSX.
The h2 and p elements display the requested text.
The component is exported as the default export.
commonMistakes: Returning sibling JSX elements without a parent.
Using plain text outside JSX elements.

title: Display Props
prompt: Build a functional component that receives a name prop and displays it in a heading.

steps: Accept props in the component parameter.
Read the name value from props.
Render the name inside a heading.
approach.example: When name is 'Samir, the heading displays 'Hello, Samir'.

walkthroughSteps: Welcome destructures the name prop from its parameter.
JSX braces insert the JavaScript value into the heading.
React renders the supplied name dynamically.
The component is exported as default.
commonMistakes: Writing {name} as plain text instead of using JSX braces.
Reading props.name after destructuring name.

title: User Card
prompt: Build a functional component that receives a name and role through props and displays them in a small card.

approach.example: With name 'Alex' and role 'Developer', the card displays both values.

walkthroughSteps: UserCard receives name and role through destructured props.
The div groups the card content.
The h2 displays name and the p displays role.
Both values change when different props are supplied.
commonMistakes: Using quoted text such as '{name}' instead of JSX expressions.
Using props.role after already destructuring role.

title: Click Counter
prompt: Build a functional component with a button that increases a displayed count whenever it is clicked.

steps: Use useState to store the count.
Add a button with a click handler.
approach.example: The count starts at 0 and changes to 1, then 2 after two button clicks.

walkthroughSteps: useState creates count with an initial value of zero.
setCount provides the function for changing count.
The button displays the current count through JSX.
Each click calls setCount with the current count plus one.
commonMistakes: Changing count directly instead of using setCount.
Calling setCount during rendering instead of inside the click handler.

title: Toggle Message
prompt: Build a functional component with a button that toggles a message between visible and hidden.

steps: Toggle the state when the button is clicked.
Render the message only when visible.
approach.example: The message is visible initially, disappears after one click, and returns after the next click.

walkthroughSteps: visible stores whether the message should appear.
The button reverses visible using setVisible.
The && expression renders the paragraph only when visible is true.
React updates the displayed JSX after the state changes.
commonMistakes: Using visible = !visible instead of the state setter.
Using a string comparison instead of a boolean state.

title: Controlled Input
prompt: Build a functional component with a controlled text input and display the current input value below it.

steps: Create state for the input value.
Connect the input value to state.
Display the current value below the input.
approach.example: Typing 'React' changes the displayed value from an empty string to 'React'.

walkthroughSteps: name stores the current input value.
The input receives name through its value prop.
onChange reads event.target.value and updates name.
The paragraph immediately reflects the updated state.
commonMistakes: Using defaultValue when a controlled input is required.
Reading event.value instead of event.target.value.

title: Submit Form
prompt: Build a small controlled form with an input and submit button that prevents the browser's default form submission.

approach.example: Typing 'React' and pressing Submit keeps the page in place because the default submission is prevented.'

walkthroughSteps: value stores the current input text.
The input updates value whenever the user types.
handleSubmit receives the form submission event.
preventDefault stops the browser from performing its normal submission.
commonMistakes: Forgetting event.preventDefault in the submit handler.
Attaching onSubmit to the button instead of the form.

title: Render A List
prompt: Build a functional component that renders a short array of names as an unordered list using map.

steps: Return one list item for each name.
Provide a key for each item.
approach.example: The array ['Sam', 'Alex'] produces two list items displaying Sam and Alex.

walkthroughSteps: names contains the values to display.
map creates one JSX list item for each name.
The name is rendered inside each li element.
key gives React a stable identifier for each list item.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the key prop on mapped list items.
Using braces around map without returning the list item.

title: Conditional Greeting
prompt: Build a component that displays a different message depending on whether a loggedIn prop is true or false.

steps: Choose a message from its boolean value.
approach.example: With loggedIn true the component displays 'Welcome back', while false displays 'Please log in'.

walkthroughSteps: Greeting receives loggedIn as a boolean prop.
The ternary checks the value of loggedIn.
The first string is selected when it is true.
The second string is selected when it is false.
commonMistakes: Using assignment instead of checking the boolean value.
Reversing the true and false messages.

title: Show Error
prompt: Build a component that displays an error message only when an error prop contains a truthy value.

steps: Render the message when error is truthy.
Render nothing when error is absent.
approach.example: With error set to 'Invalid password', the component displays that message; with an empty value, it displays nothing.

walkthroughSteps: ErrorMessage receives error through props.
The && expression checks whether error is truthy.
A truthy error produces the paragraph.
A falsy error produces no paragraph.
commonMistakes: Always rendering the paragraph regardless of error.
Using the text 'error' instead of the error prop value.

title: Toggle Theme
prompt: Build a component with a button that toggles between Light and Dark text states.

steps: Toggle the theme on button click.
approach.example: The component starts with Light, changes to Dark after one click, and returns to Light after another.

walkthroughSteps: dark stores whether the dark state is active.
The click handler reverses the dark boolean.
The ternary selects Dark or Light based on that state.
React re-renders the button text after each state update.
commonMistakes: Storing the strings Dark and Light when a boolean is enough.
Changing dark directly instead of using setDark.

title: Increment By Two
prompt: Build a component with a counter button that increases the count by two each time it is clicked.

steps: Create count state starting at zero.
Add a click handler to the button.
approach.example: The counter starts at 0 and changes to 2, then 4 after two clicks.

walkthroughSteps: count stores the current numeric value.
The initial state is zero.
The click handler adds two to count.
The button displays the updated count after each click.
commonMistakes: Adding one instead of two.
Calling setCount twice when one update is sufficient.

title: Reset Counter
prompt: Build a component with a counter and a button that resets the counter to zero.

steps: Set count back to zero when clicked.
approach.example: If the count is 5, clicking Reset changes it immediately to 0.

walkthroughSteps: count stores the current counter value.
The paragraph renders the current count.
The reset button runs setCount with zero.
React re-renders the paragraph with the reset value.
commonMistakes: Setting count to the current count instead of zero.
Calling setCount(0) while rendering rather than inside the click handler.

title: Character Counter
prompt: Build a controlled input that displays the number of characters currently typed.

steps: Create state for the input text.
approach.example: Typing 'React' produces a displayed character count of 5.

walkthroughSteps: text stores the current input content.
onChange updates text with the latest value.
text.length calculates the number of characters.
The paragraph displays the calculated length.
commonMistakes: Counting the input event object instead of the text value.
Using text.length() even though length is a property.

title: Checkbox State
prompt: Build a controlled checkbox that displays whether it is currently checked.

steps: Update state when the checkbox changes.
approach.example: The status displays 'Unchecked' initially and changes to 'Checked' after selecting the box.

walkthroughSteps: checked stores the checkbox boolean state.
The checked prop makes the input controlled.
onChange reads event.target.checked.
The ternary displays the matching status text.
commonMistakes: Reading event.target.value instead of event.target.checked.
Using value to control a checkbox.

title: Select Value
prompt: Build a controlled select element that displays the currently selected option.

steps: Create state for the selected value.
Connect value to the select element.
approach.example: Selecting 'JavaScript' changes the displayed value from 'React' to 'JavaScript'.

walkthroughSteps: language stores the selected option.
The select value is controlled by language.
onChange reads the newly selected option.
The paragraph renders the current language.
commonMistakes: Reading event.target.checked instead of event.target.value.
Leaving the select uncontrolled while expecting state to update it.

title: Show List Count
prompt: Build a component that renders an array of items and displays how many items are in the array.

approach.example: An array containing three tasks produces three list items and displays Total: 3.

walkthroughSteps: tasks stores the items that will be rendered.
tasks.length provides the total number of items.
map creates one list item for each task.
Each list item uses task as its key.
commonMistakes: Using the rendered list to calculate the count.
Forgetting a key when mapping the tasks.

title: Disable Button
prompt: Build a component with a button that is disabled when a disabled prop is true.

steps: Pass disabled to the button's disabled attribute.
approach.example: With disabled set to true the button cannot be clicked, while false keeps it enabled.

walkthroughSteps: SubmitButton receives disabled through props.
The disabled prop is passed directly to the button.
React applies the native disabled behavior when the value is true.
The button remains enabled when disabled is false.
commonMistakes: Writing disabled as a string instead of using the prop value.
Using disabled() as though it were a function.

title: Button Click Message
prompt: Build a functional component with a button that displays a message after the button is clicked.

steps: Update the message inside the click handler.
Render the message below the button.
approach.example: The component initially shows no message. Clicking the button displays Button clicked!.

walkthroughSteps: message stores the text displayed below the button.
The initial value is an empty string.
Clicking the button calls setMessage with the new text.
React re-renders the paragraph with the updated message.
commonMistakes: Changing the message variable directly.
Calling the state setter while rendering instead of inside the click handler.

title: Clear Input
prompt: Build a controlled text input with a button that clears the input value when clicked.

steps: Connect the input to the state.
Set the state to an empty string when Clear is clicked.
approach.example: If the input contains React, clicking Clear changes it back to an empty input.

walkthroughSteps: text stores the current input value.
The input is controlled through the value prop.
onChange updates text as the user types.
The Clear button resets text to an empty string.
commonMistakes: Using defaultValue instead of a controlled value.
Trying to clear the input with document.getElementById instead of React state.

title: Add List Item
prompt: Build a component with a controlled input and button that adds the typed item to a displayed list.

steps: Create state for the input text.
Update the input state while typing.
Add the input value to the list when the button is clicked.
approach.example: Typing Learn React and clicking Add adds Learn React as a new list item.

walkthroughSteps: text stores the current input.
items stores the displayed list.
addItem ignores blank input and appends valid text.
setText clears the input after a successful addition.
commonMistakes: Using items.push() directly and expecting React to re-render.
Adding empty strings to the list.

title: Remove List Item
prompt: Build a component that displays a list of items and provides a button beside each item to remove it.

steps: Map the items into list elements.
Add a remove button for each item.
Filter out the selected item when its button is clicked.
approach.example: For [HTML, CSS, React], clicking Remove beside CSS leaves HTML and React.

walkthroughSteps: items contains the current list.
map creates one list item and button for every element.
The clicked item's index is passed to removeItem.
filter creates a new array without the selected item.
commonMistakes: Using splice directly on the state array.
Removing every item instead of only the selected index.

title: Update Input Text
prompt: Build a controlled input that displays a live greeting using the text entered by the user.

steps: Insert the value into a greeting.
Render the greeting below the input.
approach.example: Typing 'May' produces the message 'Hello, Maya!'.

walkthroughSteps: name contains the latest input value.
onChange updates name on every keystroke.
The JSX expression inserts name into the greeting.
The greeting therefore changes without a separate submit action.
commonMistakes: Reading the input only after a button click.
Using literal text instead of the name expression.

title: Boolean Prop
prompt: Build a component that receives an active boolean prop and displays Active or Inactive.

approach.example: Passing active={true} displays 'Active' and active={false} displays 'Inactive'.

walkthroughSteps: Status receives active from props.
The ternary checks the boolean value.
The first string is rendered for true.
The second string is rendered for false.
commonMistakes: Comparing active to the string 'true'.
Reversing the Active and Inactive branches.

title: Default Prop Value
prompt: Build a component that displays a name prop and uses Guest when no name is provided.

steps: Provide Guest as its default value.
approach.example: Without a name prop the component displays 'Welcome, Guest'; with name='Sam' it displays 'Welcome, Sam'.

walkthroughSteps: The component destructures name from props.
The assignment gives name a fallback value when it is undefined.
JSX inserts the resulting name.
A supplied name overrides the default.
commonMistakes: Using a default value outside the destructuring incorrectly.
Replacing every falsy value when only an undefined prop needs a default.

title: Render Numbers
prompt: Build a component that renders the numbers from an array as an unordered list.

steps: Render each number inside a list item.
Use a stable key for each item.
approach.example: The array [1, 2, 3] produces three list items showing 1, 2, and 3.

walkthroughSteps: numbers contains the values to render.
map transforms each number into a list item.
The number is inserted into JSX with braces.
The number itself is used as the key because the sample values are unique.
commonMistakes: Rendering the entire array directly without mapping it.
Forgetting the key prop.

title: Filter Numbers
prompt: Build a component that displays only the even numbers from a small number array.

steps: Filter the array for even values.
Map the filtered values into list items.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 3, 4], the component displays only 2 and 4.

walkthroughSteps: numbers contains all source values.
filter keeps values whose remainder after division by two is zero.
evens contains only the qualifying numbers.
map converts those values into JSX list items.
commonMistakes: Using filter with an assignment instead of a condition.
Mapping the original numbers instead of the filtered array.

title: Component Composition
prompt: Build a parent component that renders a separate child component inside it.

steps: Render the child inside the parent.
approach.example: The parent renders a heading and a reusable Message child that displays Welcome!.

walkthroughSteps: Message is a reusable child component.
App is the parent component.
The Message component is rendered with JSX syntax.
App is exported as the default component.
commonMistakes: Calling Message() directly instead of rendering <Message />.
Forgetting that component names should begin with an uppercase letter.

title: Pass Prop To Child
prompt: Build a parent component that passes a name prop to a child component, which displays the name.

steps: Create a child component that accepts name.
Pass a name value through JSX.
Render the child inside the parent.
approach.example: The parent passes name='Sam', and the child displays Hello, Sam.

walkthroughSteps: Greeting receives name from its props.
App creates the child with name=Sam.
React passes that value into Greeting.
Greeting renders the value inside the paragraph.
commonMistakes: Using name without declaring it as a prop.
Passing the prop as plain text outside JSX.

title: Reusable Card
prompt: Build a reusable Card component that receives title and description props and renders both values.

steps: Render both values in the card.
approach.example: Passing title='React' and description='UI library' renders both pieces of content.

walkthroughSteps: Card receives two reusable pieces of data.
title is displayed as the heading.
description is displayed as paragraph content.
The same component can be reused with different props.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding the title and description instead of using props.
Mixing up the two prop names.

title: Incremental Input
prompt: Build a component where a button increases a numeric value entered in a controlled input by one.

steps: Convert the input value to a number when updating state.
Increase the value by one when the button is clicked.
approach.example: If the input contains 5, clicking Increase changes it to 6.

walkthroughSteps: number stores the numeric input value.
Number converts the input string into a number.
The button adds one to the current state.
The controlled input reflects the updated number.
commonMistakes: Concatenating strings such as 5 + 1 into 51.
Forgetting to convert event.target.value from a string.

title: Reset Form
prompt: Build a small controlled form with a text input and a Reset button that returns the input to its initial value.

steps: Create state with an initial value.
Bind the input to that state.
Reset the state when the button is clicked.
approach.example: If the initial value is 'React' and the user changes it to 'Vue', Reset returns it to 'React'.

walkthroughSteps: value begins with React.
Typing updates value through the change handler.
The Reset button sets value back to React.
Because the input is controlled, the visible value also resets.
commonMistakes: Clearing the value instead of restoring the initial value.
Using defaultValue when the reset must update the current controlled value.

title: Character Limit
prompt: Build a controlled input that prevents the user from entering more than ten characters.

steps: Create state for the input text.
Set the input maxLength to ten.
approach.example: Typing more than ten characters does not allow the input to exceed ten characters.

walkthroughSteps: text stores the controlled input value.
maxLength={10} limits the input to ten characters.
onChange keeps React state synchronized with the input.
text.length displays the current number of characters.
commonMistakes: Writing maxLength='10' as an unnecessary string value.
Counting characters from the DOM instead of React state.

title: Show Or Hide Password
prompt: Build a password input with a button that toggles between password and text input types.

steps: Use password as the initial input type.
Toggle visibility when the button is clicked.
Switch the input type based on the state.
approach.example: The input initially hides the password; clicking Show changes it to visible text, and clicking again hides it.

walkthroughSteps: visible tracks whether the password should be shown.
The ternary changes the input type between text and password.
The button reverses the visible state.
The button label also changes to match the current state.
commonMistakes: Toggling the label but not the input type.
Using text as the initial type when the password should start hidden.

title: Select Greeting
prompt: Build a controlled select with several names and display a greeting for the selected name.

steps: Create state for the selected name.
Add name options to the select.
Update state when the selection changes.
Display a greeting using the selected value.
approach.example: Selecting Maya displays 'Hello, Maya!' below the select.

walkthroughSteps: name stores the selected option.
The select is controlled by the name state.
onChange updates name from the selected option.
The paragraph uses the current name to build the greeting.
commonMistakes: Using the option index instead of its value.
Forgetting to connect the select value to state.

title: Conditional Button
prompt: Build a component that displays one button for a logged-in user and another button for a logged-out user.

approach.example: loggedIn=true displays 'Logout', while loggedIn=false displays 'Login.

walkthroughSteps: AuthButton receives the loggedIn state as a prop.
The ternary evaluates the boolean.
Logout is selected when loggedIn is true.
Login is selected when loggedIn is false.
commonMistakes: Writing two buttons instead of conditionally selecting one.
Reversing the login and logout conditions.

title: Empty List Message
prompt: Build a component that displays a list when items exist and an empty message when the list has no items.

steps: Check whether the array contains items.
Render the list when items exist.
approach.example: For an empty array the component displays 'No items'; for a non-empty array it displays the items.

walkthroughSteps: items contains the data to display.
items.length determines whether the array has elements.
A non-empty array is mapped into list items.
An empty array produces the No items message.
commonMistakes: Checking items instead of items.length.
Trying to map an empty list and expecting an empty-state message automatically.

title: Simple Todo
prompt: Build a small todo component where a user can type a task, add it to a list, and see the added tasks displayed.

steps: Create state for the input value.
Create state for the todo list.
Add non-empty tasks to the list and clear the input.
approach.example: Typing 'Practice React' and clicking Add displays 'Practice React' as a new todo item.

walkthroughSteps: task stores the current text input.
todos stores all added tasks.
addTodo ignores blank input and creates a new array with the task.
The input is cleared after the task is added.
map renders each todo as a list item.
commonMistakes: Mutating todos directly with push.
Allowing blank tasks to be added.
Forgetting to clear the input after adding a task.
